nameStory: The winter flounder gets its name because it's most active and easiest to catch during the colder months when other fish have moved to deeper waters. While many fish flee to warmer areas in winter, this hardy flatfish actually thrives in chilly New England waters, making it a favorite target for ice fishers and cold-weather anglers.
description: The winter flounder is a flat, pancake-shaped fish that spends its life lying sideways on sandy or muddy bottoms. Both eyes are located on the right side of its head (when viewed from above), allowing it to watch for predators and prey while buried in sediment. These bottom-dwellers typically grow 12-18 inches long and weigh 1-3 pounds, though some giants on Georges Bank can reach nearly 3 feet and weigh up to 8 pounds. They're the most common shallow-water flounder along New England's coast.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Completely flattened like a dinner plate, with both eyes on the right side of the head when viewed from above. The body feels firm and muscular, not squishy like a ray.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark brown to olive-green on top with the ability to change color to match the bottom, while the underside (left side) is pure white. The dark side often has a mottled pattern.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small mouth located on the underside (white side) with tiny teeth. The mouth feels rough and sandpapery when you run your finger along it.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, continuous dorsal and anal fins that run almost the entire length of the body, creating a fringe-like border. The fins feel delicate and papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found buried in sand, mud, or gravel bottoms in shallow coastal waters, often in less than 30 feet of water. Look for slight depressions or eyes poking up from the bottom.

habitat: Winter flounder live in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, preferring sandy or muddy bottoms in bays, harbors, and nearshore areas. They're commonly found in depths of 5-30 feet, often burying themselves in soft sediment with only their eyes exposed. Look for them around eelgrass beds, tidal flats, and protected coves where they hunt for marine worms, small crustaceans, and mollusks.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season brings winter flounder into very shallow waters, sometimes in just a few feet of water near shore. This is when they're most concentrated and easiest to spot.
seasonality.summer: Fish move to slightly deeper, cooler waters but remain in the nearshore zone. Young flounder that started life swimming upright begin their dramatic transformation to flatfish form.
seasonality.fall: Adults start moving back toward shallower areas as water temperatures drop. Their appetites increase as they prepare for winter, making them active feeders.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for winter flounder fishing as they're most active in cold water. They concentrate in harbors and protected bays where the water is slightly warmer.

funFact: Baby winter flounder start life swimming upright like normal fish with eyes on both sides of their head, but as they grow, one eye literally migrates across the top of their skull to join the other eye, and they flip sideways to become bottom-dwellers - it's like a real-life Pokémon evolution!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with summer flounder (fluke), but winter flounder are 'right-eyed' (eyes on the right side when dark side is up) while summer flounder are 'left-eyed.' Memory trick: Winter flounder are 'right' for cold weather. Summer flounder also have a much larger mouth with prominent teeth.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'winter' flounder, they don't actually hibernate or disappear in summer - they're called winter flounder because they're most active and catchable when the water is cold, unlike most other fish species that become sluggish in winter.
compareHints: Winter flounder is the only species in its genus Pseudopleuronectes found in New England waters. Compared to other righteye flounders in the region, winter flounder are smaller and stay in much shallower water than their deep-water cousins like yellowtail flounder. They also have a more oval body shape compared to the more elongated witch flounder, and lack the distinctive yellow tail fin that gives yellowtail flounder its name.
